t: Find Users with High Token Usage — SQL Aggregation
o: Group prompts by user, compute prompt counts and average tokens (rounded to 2 decimals), keep users with ≥ 3 prompts who also have at least one prompt exceeding their own average — equivalently MAX(tokens) > AVG(tokens) within the group. User 2 is dropped for count, users 1 and 3 qualify, ordered by average descending.
k: 'Has a prompt above personal average' simplifies to the group condition MAX(tokens) > AVG(tokens).
Filtering on aggregates belongs in HAVING; rounding happens in the SELECT.

a.i: One grouped query computes count, rounded average, and applies both aggregate filters.
s: Select COUNT(*) and ROUND(AVG(tokens), 2); order by avg_tokens DESC, user_id ASC.

c.python:
SELECT user_id,
       COUNT(*) AS prompt_count,
       ROUND(AVG(tokens), 2) AS avg_tokens
FROM prompts
GROUP BY user_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
   AND MAX(tokens) > AVG(tokens)
ORDER BY avg_tokens DESC, user_id ASC;

a.t: O(N log N) — single grouped scan plus sort, N = rows

w: Single clean query; no joins needed. Pitfall: trying to reference the alias avg_tokens inside HAVING (not portable — repeat the aggregate), and forgetting that MAX > AVG is exactly the 'above-average prompt exists' condition. Follow-up: users whose maximum exceeds 1.5× their average, or per-month breakdowns.
